p:
Yeah, I just wanted to highlight that because that was something that the young people kind of like talked about and I’m real big on making sure that we’re highlighting what young people are saying and the needs of them and that was a clear reaction of young people saying like, formal

therapy we’ve been doing for our entire lives. We want to try something else and ACS responding to that and listening and being able to uhm, counter that. So, thank you and I just wanted to get that on record. Next, uhm, person, Council Member Joseph.

We were plotting as usual on behalf of the kids. You know. Thank you Chair. Good morning to each and every one of you. My first question, I’m going to deviate a little bit. Transportation for foster youth, that’s something I've been fighting for for a long time. And if you look at the data, it doesn’t look really good. 55 percent of our youth in foster care are absent because of transportation once they enter into care and you know I know this personally. So, how are we going to look at transportation for foster youth? I know it’s a $3 million investment that we’re been asking for. How do we plan to address transportation for youth and how closely are you working with the New York City Public Schools Office in foster care to make sure that we are alleviating that?
Is it still morning? Good morning Council Member Joseph.
Yes Ma’am.

So, yes so we do work very closely with the New York City foster care office. In 2022, early 2023, we launched a foster care transportation reimbursement agreement, which we did not have in place before and that outlines how foster care providers can be reimbursed for the transportation. And it allows for trips up to ten days and the hope is that within that period, up to $200 and the idea is that within ten days, children will be assigned to a bus route but that does not always happen.
That doesn’t happen.

Right and so we are now having additional conversations. So, our finance team, we’ve talked internally. We actually have a meeting with New York City Public Schools this Friday to figure out how best to kind of expand this transportation agreement. There are some challenges. What they’ve shared, so through our conversations, so through our conversations with them that you know there are these placements and where the school is

there’s not a clear bus route. And so, how do we solve that? Because we want the children to get to school obviously or prioritizing placing with kin. So, maybe the kin live in a different borough but we want the kids to go to the school of origin. So, there are some nuances. So, we have a meeting this Friday. There was a meeting that uhm, the past Friday, I missed a meeting with the advocates. So, we are talking to our stakeholders and partnering with New York City Public Schools and then we’re talking internally how to identify a - the logistics around what is the service? Is it a rideshare? Is it some type of agreement with maybe another type of bus company that can provide it and then we’ll just try to identify next steps. So, we’re aware of the issue, we’re just trying to piecemeal it out and figure out how to best tackle it.

It’s been an issue since I was a foster mom. It has been an issue since I adopted my boys. So, it’s been an ongoing issue and even when I became a Council Member, it was - and that was why I was so strategic to create that office

to make sure that we are providing transportation for our foster youth right. Not everybody is going to be like, nope we’re going to go the same - you’re going to go the same school that I was teaching at so you don’t have a transportation issue but not every parent has that. So, we want to make sure that and the data for our foster youth and absenteeism rate is too high. It’s 55 percent. We need to bring that down in terms of transportation and the first ten days when they are placed in care, they should not be home or somewhere else. So, this is lived experience, not speaking from a third party. This is lived experience. So, my first question is around child center staff and support service new needs. Your preliminary plan includes an additional $3 million from mixed city, state, federal funding in Fiscal 2026. $4 million in the Fiscal 2027 growing to $4.2 million by Fiscal 2030 for staff support services at the Child Center. Additionally, the funding supports 13 new baseline positions. Can you tell me what programs or services does this relate to?
Thank you for this important question. First Deputy Commissioner Saunders will take it.

Good morning Council Member Joseph. Thank you so much for that question. It is of critical importance to us to provide quality and care for our young people at the Children’s Center. With that being said, the investments that you spoke of really focus on strengthening our medical, mental health support, operational capacity and safety and security of the center. A large portion of that is focused on chaperones, just like you mentioned earlier around transportation. We take very seriously that we want to make sure that kids maintain their community ties, so regardless of what school that child went to or goes to, we take that child to their community school. So, we are ensuring that we have enough chaperones to maintain those community ties at school but also medical appointments, also recreational visits, also visits and court. So, a lot of that is baked into that. With that being said, we also have money that is focused on our

medical consultation. We want our nurses and we also have mental health supports. Right now we have four child psychologists, two psychiatrists and we want an additional mental health enhancement there as well.
So, why is the additional funding required and what was the amount? Do you have a number?
The amount -
Determined for this.
The additional amounts were $0.2 million.
Were $0.2, thank you and what operational costs will this funding cover? What portion of them relate to the contracted providers?

So, for the children at the Children’s Center, they’re not yet with one of the contracted providers, so this is funding for the most part for our team. It also does go to Bellevue uhm for the mental health and the chaperones are contracted out.
It’s contracted out, okay.
Yeah, this is specifically for the children who reside at the Children’s Center.
Okay, thank you. We needed that on the record.
You’re welcome.
So what positions are being added and what would that responsibility look like?
Okay so I have the actual list. So, we have one behavioral health position, which I spoke of earlier. One Deputy Director of intake and we have 11 for peace officers.
Okay and what positions currently staff at the Children’s Center now?
Oh well, that's a long list.
That’s a long list. You’ll get back to us. Chair.
No, no, I know them.
You know them, alright.
I do know them.
Alright.

So, we have nurses. We have uhm the doctors that I spoke of that are part of the mental health team from Bellevue. We have a

childcare staff. We have childcare supervisors. We have social workers. We have a team of programming specialists who really focus on the reduction of idle time and supporting young people and engaging them in positive activities. We also have temps that assist us with supervision onsite and the chaperoning as we spoke of earlier. We also have a transportation team and we also have peace officers and I think I covered most.

Well, thank you that is. Now I’m going to head over to our justice - our Juvenile Justice Staff and support service new need. We held a hearing not too long ago, a matter of fact, two hearings I think, Council Member Stevens, Chair Stevens. We held two hearings around justice involved youth. How is it looking now? I know it’s overcrowded. Our plan is to bring down the population. How many of our students are now receiving full classes and getting their full services?
So, Deputy Commissioner Ginsberg, do you want to talk a little bit about education?

So, we’ve set up a split schedule for the young people so that the high school students go in the morning and GED students receive their services between 3 and 6, so that we could increase the number of young people accessing services. Generally the GED students, if they are willing to attend that day, are going - we’re seeing very good retention rates for GED students. Uhm, about 80 percent of the high school students are attending. Uhm, we have a number of supports that we have put into place to support these students. So, we have tutoring that is provided by our partners, providing workforce development. They also provide tutoring services. We have recently started an algebra tutoring service because it is an area that our young people historically have struggled with -
Across the city.

Across the city, correct. So, we are hoping that we see increased pass rates on the Regents due to this intervention. The kids are very excited about it and they have been attending. The attending rates are very good for that tutoring.

We also have uhm working very, very closely with our Passages Academy partners from New York City Public Schools. They have increased literacy supports. Uhm, they are running Saturday school now for young people to receive their related services, increased literacy services and Regents prep.

That was going to be my next question, our students with IEP. That was one of the population that was not getting none of the services when we had this hearing here, so I just wanted to hear our students with IEP’s. How are they getting their related services? Are there make up times for our students with IEP’s?

So, uhm District 79 has worked very hard to identify staff outside of Passages Academy and they come in; there’s a separate set of teachers and providers that come in on Saturdays and the young people who have related services receive those related services other than counseling, which they receive during the week from Passages Academy stuff. So, if they have speech or any other type of related service that is not provided during the week by passages, this additional team is providing those services on Saturdays.
I know our Chair will make a visit soon. So -

Before you move on, can I just go back to your last question on foster youth. We have the attendance rates for youth and foster care ages 5 to 10 at 91 percent and 11 to 15 at 86 percent. I just wanted to clarify that.
I was specifically talking about young people that did not have transportation. That’s the data, if you pull it up we can see it black and white.
Got it. Okay, thank you.
That’s the youth that I was referring to in terms of transportation.
Got it, thank you.

Thank you. The Preliminary Plan includes an additional $4.6 million in city funding and 33 positions in Fiscal 2026 and a baseline addition of $8.1 million along with 40 positions, starting in Fiscal 2027 for juvenile justice staff and support services. What programs or services is this related to?

I’ll start and then Deputy Commissioner Ginsberg can add. Uhm, part of the

staff is seven additional staff for the new exercise pavilion, which will be open and we’re very excited about but it’s three levels. It needs additional staff and the rest is for additional security staff for both facilities.
Your additional funding requires, what’s the amount determined for your additional? Is it the $4.6 million or the $8.1 million, which one?
Thank you. What operational costs will the funding cover? What portion of them is related to the contract providers?

So, most of the detention again is similar to the Children’s Center operated directly by ACS, although we do contract out for example, for programming, the barbers, the contract out so that’s included in the funding. I don’t know if you want to add.
Okay, and what positions are being added to this and what are their main responsibilities?
It’s mostly security and the Exercise Pavillion. Uhm, do you want to talk more about -
There’s some increase for cleaning.
And what’s the timeline -
Titles -
Go ahead.
Uhm, it’s 16 special officers for one facility 16 special officers and one sergeant special officer.
And what’s the timeline for hiring for these new positions?
As soon as we can.
What is it?
We’ll be working on that as soon as we can.
And you’ll let the Committee know. Thank you. Thank you Chair.

Thank you Council Member Joseph. Council Member Gutiérrez. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you Chair. I also just want to lend my support to uhm, Chair Joseph on her advocacy for the transportation for

foster youth. She’s a wonderful advocate, constantly reminding the Council to really uplift that. So, I know you’ll be hearing from some advocates today that also agree with that and I just want to make sure that I support her and uplift that. I have some questions related to uhm, the vouchers and I know you touched on it in your testimony and so did Chair Stevens but I just want to make sure that we didn’t cover it. Were you able today, this morning to share the amount of children that are currently on the waitlist?

Sure, it’s approximately $17,000 but Deputy Commissioner Wolkimer is going to take your childcare voucher questions. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Excellent, thank you okay so around $17,000. Uhm, how many childcare vouchers has ACS administered to new clients on cash assistance since the reintroduction of work requirements?

ACS doesn’t administer cash assistance to families or doesn’t administer childcare assistance to families on cash assistance. HRA does that, so they would have those numbers.

COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: So, you don’t have those numbers?
No. I have the current number of children enrolled that are on cash and using childcare assistance but I don’t have - COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: The new numbers?

The difference based on the work requirements. As of the end of January, there were about 29,000 children enrolled in cash assistance or in childcare assistance that uncashed. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Okay, vouchers with cash, okay and are you able to - those are the numbers from January you said?
End of January. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: End of January, okay have you seen the growth? Have you seen the rate grow month to month?

There has been modest growth month to month. HRA is still projecting and of course they will be able to tell you more what’s behind their projections but still projecting over the next months a steeper growth curve but end of January was about $29,000 children and that is up from about $27,000 for example last April.

COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Wow, okay.
So, slow growth. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Okay and do you think that those numbers pair up with what ACS maybe projected?

HRA does those projections and we are in close communication with them every month about what those look like but we don’t hold those projections. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Okay. Does - and I think - let me just ask it so that I have it on record. Does ACS, I know you’re in communication with HRA. Can you share any projection of the childcare vouchers? The projection of the number of new cash assistance clients that will provide childcare vouchers by the time work requirements are fully reintroduced by this time next year.

I think they’d have to give those most recent projections. The last time we spoke with them though, they do expect it to rise significantly so tens of thousands more children but they should weigh in on the exact projection and rate of increase that they expect.

COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Okay, can you share what the breakdown of the ages are for children on the waitlist, the 17,000 or so?
I don’t have that with me but we can certainly share that. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Okay and do you have a sense of whether or not some of these children may or may not still need the vouchers?

We know that uhm, many children on the waitlist are getting care from DOE or DYCD afterschool programs. We don’t have perfect information on all of that. The way that the childcare assistance program works is that if a family applies, they have an opportunity to seek a voucher or to be enrolled in contracted care. So, it may be and is the case that many children that have applied with the intention of being in a DOE contracted seat are in one of those seats, however, those children remain on the waitlist, so that if a parent, if we reach them on the waitlist at a future moment and that parent wants to select a voucher, they can.

COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Okay and do you - when did basically you stop allowing or granting vouchers to families on the waitlist?
We were providing vouchers to any child or any child of a family that applied and was found eligible up through May 5th. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Of last year?

Of last year. So, up till that point, there was no waitlist at all. At that point and time given where we were on the budget and where the budget landed in the state process, we began the waitlist at that time, which has now grown to about 17,000 children and uhm and we implemented a policy to recertify the vast majority of families that are currently receiving vouchers. So, we really are prioritizing right now continuity of care - COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Sustaining families, yeah and understand the challenges. Uhm, what - do you have a sense of what your projection would be to end the waitlist?

We don’t for a couple of reasons. As we just talked about, we don’t know exactly what takeup would be as we started to move through the waitlist because some families have their

children in other arrangements and may decide at that point that a voucher is not necessary. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: But you’re not aware of family to family on that 17,000 who those families are?

We know some that are enrolled in DOE care but we don’t know the universe or totality of arrangements that families have made. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: But are you all working to kind of figure that out in communication with families? Like what is the way to basically like update this waiting list so that you have a sense of -

Well, they’re going to work with us to get us a list of different scenarios that they promised that they’re going to work with us to do different scenarios for a one to have different ones, whether they’re in the childcare and things like that, so.

We will work on what projections of different take up from the waitlist would be. What I will say though is that families have a right to remain on the waitlist, so we would

never remove someone from the waitlist just because they have other - COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: No, no, I’m not implying that. I just want to make sure I think there are families on that waitlist that are like have not been communicating - are not even sure like kind of where they are on that waitlist. So, I just, I want to understand the communication with families once they’re made aware that they’re on a waitlist. I understand you guys are trying to figure out you know, it’s possible they are not eligible for an ECEC. I just want to understand how that communication is with a family who is on the waitlist. How often is it? How are you emailing, calling, texting?

We’re emailing. Uhm, we have been emailing and mailing about opportunities to enroll in 3K, PreK. We did that very recently with 3K, PreK enrollments in that cycle closing and about DYCD openings for after school and so, we are doing that on a regular rhythm. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Chair, I just have one more question. Thank you. Uhm, and at the Subcommittee for Early Childhood Committee Meeting I

think earlier this month, we got from both the DOE’s Early Childhood Division and the Office for Childcare that there is, you know, consistent communication with ACS, with DOH, with DOB where it’s multiple times a week. Can you just share with me uhm, I guess how that communication is then being shared to families? Like does ACS take a role in communicating these like childcare updates with families? How does that look like? Is it just a text? I want to make sure we’re not missing folks. I know the Administration did a ton of outreach, link kiosks, radio, social media, all that stuff, just kind of what is the role that ACS plays in that?

Yeah, I mean we do push out communication to families. Some of our mechanisms are imperfect because we don’t have phone numbers for everyone. We don’t have emails for everyone. That is really up to whether or not parents have provided that through their application process. Uhm, but to the extent that we do have that information, we are pushing out information and if not, unfortunately, it’s old school mailing but we are trying to reach them in that way.

The other thing I’ll say is that we are working, we worked over the past year with funding from the Robinhood Foundation with a few community based organizations to be supporting families and connecting to care and now that we are in a little bit of a different policy place, we are working with community based organizations in the Bronx and then potentially expanding uhm to be working with families that are recertifying for care and so, in that way, we are testing ways to get much closer to families, so using credible CBO’s that have a relationship already with families to either help them recertify with ACS and make sure that they are not falling away as you’re mentioning and if they no longer remain eligible for ACS care to try and connect them somewhere else in the system. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: And then my last question on that, is there a role that ACS plays in engaging with families in shelters to assess their eligibility? I know that the Administration at my hearing had said, there’s a lot of you know they took responsibility. There’s a lot more work to be done there, so just curious, is ACS involved in that, like targeted outreach to families?

When we were able - uhm, when we didn’t have a waitlist, we were working with DHS to train staff on childcare eligibility. Now that families would be applying to get on the waitlist, we are less proactively asking families to apply for care because we don’t want them to apply for a voucher and then be waiting. So, we have stepped back from that role a little bit and are more focused on making sure that families receiving care are recertifying. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: But there are scenarios where there’s families in shelters that may qualify and not need to be on cash assistance, correct?
No. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Okay, they’re all in need of the cash assistance voucher?

So, a family that is currently receiving a voucher recertifies as unhoused would absolutely remain eligible in receiving their voucher but a family applying new would not be able to. They would be on the waitlist.

COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Okay, great. Thank you so much and this is great. Send it over digitally so we can promote. Thank you guys.
We will do that. Thank you. They just got released from last week or so. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: I mean this is a cute baby. You guys did it.
Our team will be very proud. CHAIRPERSON STEVENS:Council Member Felder.
Good morning and thank you for listening to the questions. You’ve been thanking us and telling us that it was a good question. So far all of the questions we’ve asked have been good questions.
This is going to be a big test then for your question.
No, it doesn’t matter. I don’t want to take any changes. So, thank you for the thank you in advance.
You’re welcome.

Yeah, I have a slew of questions that are in no order whatsoever. So, I’m sorry I can’t you know give you the bunch and wait for an answer. So, question number one, in terms of

the cases, you know I would say that more than half of the testimony were related to foster, you know care so at this point in Family Court, those cases, when does Family Court close?
I believe it’s 5:00 p.m..

Yeah, I believe so also. So, I know it’s not your responsibility but I just want to tell you that I’ve been advocating together with many of my colleagues. If somebody gets arrested, they will be processed till 12;00 a.m.. I’m just - that I know.
On the juvenile side too right?
Yeah, yeah.
Yeah.

Right, the point that I’m trying to make is that if in criminal court, they’re open till midnight and in Family Court you have and again, this is not a case - this is an easy one you know. It’s not your responsibility. I’m just suggesting that since you’ve advocated - you advocate for so many other things you’ve talked about, so I would ask you to advocate for one more thing, which is that families that come into Family Court after

5:00, that’s the end of it. And anyone here knows that if you want to for example, when I'm in the mood to do work, you get the most work done you know on a Sunday morning when there’s no calls coming in or after 5:00 you know. You know when there’s nothing going on. So, not only is it not open after 5:00 you know, so uh and we’ve done research and there are many employees, whether it’s judges, whether it’s other employees that are necessary, that would be very interested in the flex time. You know it would allow many of them to have another job easily instead of having to, you know, take a job at night, an extra job. They would be working, so I’m just asking you to advocate for that because it seems unconscionable that a family you know that’s waiting around, waiting around has to wait around another day to get help. I’m not looking for an answer.

I’m just going to say we could take that back. We can take back that uhm, suggestion. We operate 24/7 and I know that there are a lot of challenges in the you know late shift and operating our child protection, the Children Center Detention but we can take that back and look at it.

Yeah, I thought you would just say that’s a good question and we will advocate for that but this is the story of my life. I was never a good student, so it doesn’t matter to me. I know it’s a good thing but take it back and please whoever it is, if it’s not your responsibility, I would appreciate knowing who it is so that I can drive them nuts. Okay, second thing I wanted to ask you about is you mentioned the vocational program and again, this is an easy one. The - I’m just mentioning you know again to perhaps advocate to your peers in you know education. The New York City Public School system used to have a significant vocational program option. They still give you know tests and you know they - okay, yeah -
Go ahead, you can go.
Should I shut up?
No, no, you can go. You’re doing very good, go ahead.
Yeah.
Yes, very well.
Okay, yeah. So, you have to give me extra time for the jokes.
I got you. I got you.

Okay, yeah, that doesn’t count. The point being is that the city’s public school system has very, very few options and they can give the same students the tests over and over and over. They’re just never going to do well. I know personally from experience, a student named Simcha Felder, that was in the principals office when I was lucky and not thrown out, all the time and if I had had that opportunity, I would have done extraordinarily well. You know, even though my wife says that I don’t know what I’m doing but I know that you know, it's just obvious. It’s very obvious. No - necessary, it’s a good point and you’ll take it back to whoever it is and let me know who it is, that’s all.
I will say I feel like you’ve done very well for yourself as both a Council Member and a former Senator.

I don’t know about that. All it means is that I really you know fooled a lot of people, that’s all. Yeah, so that’s question number two.

Question number three is or point number three, this does have to do with something you mentioned about Rikers numbers. So, I just will tell you is that my background for the first ten years is that I’m a CPA, even though I never liked doing it but that’s something I was able to do. The numbers, you know you can fix numbers anyway you want or at least I can fix numbers anyway you want me to, right? The numbers are really the reduction that you talk about. I’m certainly not suggesting that anyone is intentionally trying to fix the numbers. All I would say to you is that whether it’s fortunate or unfortunate, when I speak to the precincts that are within my you know, my district and I talk about different issues, a lot of the arrests or other things that normally for years would wind up in Rikers, are just not happening, for quite some time. So, I’m not suggesting that it’s not so. All I’m suggesting is that unfortunately or unfortunately there are many you know kids out that are really doing things that may be - that would wind them up in Rikers and it just it’s just not uh, you know the

arrests aren’t being made. You don’t have to comment on that because there’s no way you can.
Well, I’ll comment. I’ll just say that if that’s the case, then that’s a failure on our part for not having preventative services and preventing them from being arrested. So, I’ll comment.
Oh, okay. So, if you can take that back to whoever you have to - yeah, I think that’s -
We also support preventative services.

Yeah, no, I mean that’s what they said. I mean that’s what the cops are saying you know in the precincts. I’m not suggesting that you know that it’s - I’m not suggesting that the numbers are entirely full. All I’m saying is that unfortunately or fortunately that’s part of it. And then, the final - finally, I just wanted to say is that when you talked originally, you talked about the making sure one of the first things about the safety, you know with window guards, all of those things and educating them, whatever else, it’s a wonderful thing to educate people but I would say on the whole and

again from personal experience, I’m talking about Simcha Felder, you can educate me all day long. I probably will not do what you want me to do unless I have to. So, and today, it seems to me that almost everybody has a smart phone or access to one, and I don’t think it would be a difficult thing you know in the recertification for someone to have to - if - do you have - are there windows in your apartment, which probably is true. If so, please attach a photo of the windows with the window guards. You know if you want to make sure and I agree that the safety is critical, all I’m suggesting is that sometimes that’s the only way you will get what you want to get and it is critical because almost every year we unfortunately you know have cases of somebody getting hurt.

I hear you. It is incredibly important that people know - to have window guards and how to get window guards. At the same time, we have had a lot of feedback about the childcare application already being challenging. I don’t think combining the two is necessarily the way to ensure people are able to apply for childcare timely and that they have window guards but your idea of

ensuring that where you have a parent somewhere and they’re listening to you, that that’s the time to make sure they know how to do these things or how to access them. I think that’s really important and we can you know, Deputy Commissioner Wolkimer has a team focused on that and it’s definitely important to us.
Alright, well, that means the last one was not a good point without you saying it. And finally -
Finally okay, you’re not done, okay.
I wanted to compliment you.
Oh well thank you. Well, go ahead. I’ll let you keep going on with that.

Yeah, the first thing I wanted to say, is that it’s a really, I'm speaking for myself. If I would not be here this morning, I would not be concerned in any way about the Council, you know taking care of making sure to protect children in the city because the Chair of this Committee is someone that does not let anything go by that she is you know determined to make sure is taken care of except that they have to first of all on the

stationary it doesn’t look good if I don’t have any committees. So, they had pity and you know they put me on some Committees. I’m just saying to you that I have no question that - so, I’m humbled to be able to be on this Chairs Committee. And then finally, I just wanted to say is that we - I think we - I want to thank you for all the work you do. In other words, you come to a hearing and all you here forget about I’m not thanking you for the questions, especially with your criticism of my last point but all I wanted to say clearly is that I think that you understand that we appreciate even those people that are going to come and testify later vociferously upset and angered by something that you’re doing wrong and you might by the way, be doing something wrong. You might but there is no question that everyone appreciates the work that you’re doing and uh you know but that’s the nature of why you’re here and even as a Council Member and an elected official, it’s very rare, very rare that somebody calls or writes and says, “thank you very much.
